title: Luther's hammer
hookLine: in 1517 a monk posted 95 theses; he said we're saved by grace through faith

cards: October 31, 1517. Wittenberg, a small university town in Germany.

A thirty-three-year-old monk and professor named Martin Luther has written ninety-five short arguments, in Latin, against the sale of indulgences: letters people bought believing they would shorten the punishment due for sin in purgatory, for themselves or for loved ones who had died.
A preacher named Tetzel was selling them nearby, and people were paying. The story goes that Luther nailed them to the castle church door with a hammer. Historians argue about the hammer.
What's certain: he mailed them to his archbishop that same day. He wanted a debate among scholars. Instead, printers copied them, and soon they spread across Germany, in German too.

teach.b: The Reformation is the movement that began with Luther and reshaped Western Christianity in the 1500s. Reform means to form again, to bring back into shape.
Luther didn't set out to start a new church; he wanted to reform his own. Under the argument about indulgences lay a question that had tormented him for years.
He'd been a desperately serious monk, confessing for hours, never sure he'd done enough to stand before a holy God.

teach.h: THE JUST SHALL LIVE BY FAITH.
teach.b: Then, reading Paul's letter to the Romans, he fastened on one line, "The just shall live by faith," and said it felt like the gates of paradise opening. Righteousness wasn't something to earn. It was a gift.
Ephesians puts it in one sentence: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God."

teach.h: BY GRACE, FAITH, AND SCRIPTURE ALONE.
teach.b: From that grew convictions later summed up in Latin slogans: by grace alone, by faith alone, by scripture alone.
Luther translated the Bible into German so ordinary people could read it, and wrote hymns for whole congregations to sing.
The Catholic Church answered at the Council of Trent.

teach.h: FOR BY GRACE ARE YE SAVED THROUGH FAITH.
teach.b: Catholics also taught, and teach, that salvation is God's gift of grace, but they understood faith, works and the church's role differently, and the two sides condemned each other. Wars followed, and the West was divided.
Centuries later, Catholics and Lutherans have found they agree on more than their ancestors thought.

how: Lutheran and some other Protestant churches keep October 31 as Reformation Day, often singing Luther's hymn "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God," and preach on grace, faith and scripture.

p: the just shall live by faith
the line that set Luther free

games.q: you're a monk who confesses for hours and never feels you've done enough. you're reading Romans. what line changes everything?
o: the just shall live by faith.
games.why: Luther said "the just shall live by faith" felt like the gates of paradise opening: righteousness was a gift, not a wage.

practice: Read Ephesians 2:8 slowly, three times: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.

Then hold one thing you know you didn't earn, a person, a morning, a second chance, like a gift, not a wage. If you pray, give thanks for grace; if not, rest in the idea that not everything has to be earned.

wordCard.voice: Reformation. The movement, begun by Martin Luther in 1517, to bring the Western church back into shape around grace, faith and scripture.

orig.note: Greek: grace, a free gift, favor. The word in Ephesians 2:8, and the root of charity and charisma.

carryVoice: Your line: by grace, through faith. That one line set a monk free. That's day two hundred eighty-nine.
